- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

## plugin:small-business:shopify
This server helps users set up and manage their Shopify stores.

## Starting a New Business
Users who are still shaping a business can work on it here before they have a store. None of these tools needs one.
- Naming: generate-business-names suggests business names from a short description of what the user sells, who it is for, or the feeling they want.
- Domains: generate-domain-names checks whether a name or domain idea is available and what it costs to register, and suggests available alternatives.
When the user settles on a name, offer to check domains for it.
Never present a domain as available unless generate-domain-names checked it; a domain you suggest yourself may already be taken.
Follow the user's lead rather than walking them through every step.

## Store Creation
Users who don't have a store yet can use get-new-store-previews to create one from a short description.
After calling get-new-store-previews, encourage the user to browse the previews and pick the theme they like best.
Each preview has a signup link — signing up through it creates a real Shopify store with that theme and matching products pre-installed.
Encourage continued brainstorming: users can try different descriptions, tweak ideas, or explore new directions without commitment.

## Store Management
Once a store exists, this server provides tools for managing it:
- Products: search, create, update, bulk-update status, and organize into collections.
- Collections: search, create, update, and manage product groupings.
- Orders: list recent orders and get detailed order information.
- Customers: list and search customers.
- Inventory: check inventory levels and set quantities at specific locations.
- Analytics: run ShopifyQL queries for sales, order, and product performance data.
- Discounts: create percentage-based discount codes.

# Solo License: implementation plan for winning (v2)

*11 Oct 2026 · `main` @ `d852fb6` (after PRs #15 and #16) · Submission: **Mon 12 Oct, 7:00–11:55 PM IST***

This is a **plan only**, with no code. v2 replaces the plan written at `e1e4910`. It takes into account the 7 commits that landed on `origin/main` since then, says what they finished, what they broke, and what to do next, in order.

---

## 0. What changed on `main` since v1

| Commit | Author | What it did | Effect on the plan |
|---|---|---|---|
| `19b1330` | Swyam | neatlogs Doctor probe runs in an isolated child process; structured codes (`AUTH_FAILED`, `TRACE_READBACK_TIMEOUT`, …) | The onboarding neatlogs **Test** button works now. B1 (dashboard screenshots) is unblocked |
| `ae6b8b6` | Swyam | Onboarding is atomic; re-handling a handled ticket returns **409** instead of demoting | A1 (multi-turn) must create a *new* linked ticket, never re-handle the old one |
| `b0b9bba` | Swyam | Frontend maps probe codes to plain guidance | Done, nothing to add |
| `7d40d25` | Vansh | **Versioned policies + single-use execution permits** (`domain/policy.py`, `services/policy_gate.py`, `policy_service.py`, `PolicyEditor.jsx`, `docs/policy-governance.md`) | **A7 is done** (rules are now data, editable, versioned). New demo beat: an unauthorized write is blocked at the permit boundary |
| `218710c` | Vansh | Permits enforced inside Local and Stripe connectors | Same; also makes E3 (MCP server) much easier: it can hand out permits |
| `12ada5f` | Vansh | "features": commits `artifacts/evidence_report.*`, removes 11 lines from `frontend/package-lock.json` | `artifacts/` is now tracked (conflicts with v1 F item). Vague commit message |
| `e7951c9` | Swyam | README em dashes → hyphens | Two em dashes came back in the new README section |

**Verified now:** `python -m pytest` → **161 passed** (was 117). Frontend: **11/11** tests pass, build OK, JS chunk **723 kB** (was 712 kB).

**Local main:** fast-forwarded to `d852fb6`. The two untracked local `artifacts/evidence_report.*` files (older regenerated copies) were moved to the session scratchpad so the merge could run; the committed versions from `12ada5f` are now in place.

**Stash:** `stash@{0}` (A1 work in progress: `db/database.py`, `db/repositories/tickets.py`) was made on the old base. Both files were touched by the new commits (`database.py` got policy columns), so expect a small conflict on `git stash pop`.

---

## 1. New problems the commits introduced (fix first)

### P1. ⚠️ Promotion no longer uses the economics (highest priority)
**What happened:** in the worker path, `LicenseService.record_clean_run(..., evaluation=...)` now promotes when `evaluate_runs()` says *"≥ minimum_samples and pass rate ≥ minimum_verified_pass_rate"*. The Beta-posterior / break-even rule in `domain/trust.py` is only used when `evaluation is None`, which the worker never passes.
**Why it matters:** the README's headline differentiator, *"promotion priced by economics … upper credible bound below break-even"* and *"759 more double-checked jobs"*, is no longer what the agent actually does. A judge who reads `worker.py` → `license_service.py` will see a fixed sample count. This is also exactly what the 30% agent criterion and the cfo.ai story rest on.
**Plan:** make policy eligibility **AND** the economic bound both required:
- `eligible = policy minimums met AND Beta upper bound (computed only from this policy version's outcomes) < break-even target for this step`.
- Keep the policy's minimums as a *floor* the owner sets; the economics stays the *ceiling* nobody can lower by editing a policy.
- `EvaluationProgress` gains the "jobs still needed by the economics" number, so Home keeps showing the "759 more…" sentence alongside the policy's sample/pass-rate progress.
- Promotion reason in the ledger names both: *"policy v3 minimums met; failure rate below 0.25% with 95% confidence."*

**Files:** `sololicense/domain/policy.py` (`evaluate_runs`), `domain/trust.py` (reuse, no change), `services/policy_service.py` (`evaluation_for`), `services/license_service.py`, `api/app.py` (`serialize_evaluation`), `frontend/.../Overview.jsx`.
**Verify:** new unit tests: (a) 3/3 clean with `minimum_samples=3` does **not** promote when the Beta bound is above break-even; (b) promotes once both hold; (c) evidence from an older policy version still never counts. Full `pytest`.
**Effort:** 1.5 hours · **Risk:** medium (touches the promotion path; keep `test_policy_service.py` green).

### P2. README regressions
- Line 193–194: the *"Live Stripe keys are refused…"* line is duplicated.
- Two em dashes reintroduced in the new section (*"writes a plan — it never…"*), against PR #16's intent.
- The *"Who it is for"* table was inserted directly under the heading, above the paragraph it belongs with; reorder.
- *"Tests: `python -m pytest` - 117 tests"* → 161.

Anthropic launched auto mode for Claude Code as a research preview in March 2026, and it has since expanded.

**Launch (March 2026):** Anthropic's announcement introduced auto mode as a permissions setting where Claude makes permission decisions itself, with safeguards watching each action before it runs. Anthropic PBC announced on March 24, 2026 that it is launching "auto mode" for Claude Code. At first it was limited to the Team plan, and coming to the Enterprise plan and API users in the coming days.

**How the classifier works:** Before each tool call runs, a classifier checks it for risks such as mass deleting files, sensitive data exfiltration, or malicious code execution. Safe actions go through, while risky ones are blocked and Claude is steered toward another approach. If Claude keeps attempting blocked actions, the user gets a permission prompt.

**Limitations:** Anthropic said auto mode reduces risk compared to --dangerously-skip-permissions but doesn't eliminate it entirely, and it recommends isolated environments. The classifier can still miss risky actions when user intent is unclear or when Claude lacks context about the environment.

**Later changes:** According to The Register, auto mode became generally available on July 10. The same report says it became the default in Claude Code from August 14 for new sessions on Pro, Max, and Team plans, while it will remain opt-in for now on Claude Enterprise, the Claude API and several cloud platforms. I couldn't confirm these later dates against Anthropic's own materials, so check the current Claude Code docs before relying on them.

The query points to **Jev**, a "System One" decision model from TypeSafe AI, and its API. It returns typed answers (a boolean probability, a choice, or a score) instead of generated text.

**What the API offers**
- **Noul (boolean):** It returns a single value p in [0,1], the probability that a condition is true. The vendor's own page describes it as the basic building block for filters and guardrails.
- **Choice:** Picks one option from a fixed set and returns the full probability distribution plus confidence. It's aimed at routing and tool selection.
- **Score:** Grades input against an ordered rubric you define, with a per-level distribution. The vendor positions it for triage, risk, and quality scoring.

Requests take the form of a state plus a set of typed questions. A reviewer notes that Jev answers every question independently of the others, so one request can carry several questions.

**Latency and pricing claims conflict**
The vendor page lists 70 to 500 milliseconds per request. A third-party developer guide claims typical latencies between 11ms and 35ms. The pricing is listed as $0.042 per million input tokens, output tokens free, per the vendor's docs. One paper cites the launch materials as vendor launch claims. Quoted, not adopted. Treat these figures as unverified until you test them yourself.

**Caveats on "type-safe"**
- A critical review argues that the public benchmark is a model-agreement test rather than verified ground truth, and says the "zero hallucinations" framing is a narrow type-safety claim.
- An arXiv paper titled "Type-Safe Is Not Error-Free" examines Choice-type decisions. Its finding, from the title, is that the constrained decision head can follow the option name rather than the rubric attached to it, so type safety does not guarantee correct answers.
- The review recommends keeping a human in the loop for agent safety gates, and says invoice processing should not be automated from agreement scores alone.

**Practical implications**
Type safety means the output has a valid shape, such as one of the allowed options or a number between 0 and 1. It does not mean the answer is correct. Thresholds on the returned probabilities can gate automatic actions versus human review, but you should validate those thresholds against labeled ground truth in your own domain.

I found several open-source projects that use Claude Code hooks to auto-approve commands, but none clearly "learns" trusted commands on its own. The closest is chook, which builds rules from your usage through a review interface.

**Closest match: chook.** It is a PreToolUse hook for Claude Code that gives you granular control over what Claude can do, with an interactive review TUI for building rules from real usage. Its rules are checked in order: deny rules first as a hard block, then allow rules, which are auto-approved with no prompt. Rules are maintained by you through the review TUI, so the "learning" is human-guided rather than automatic.

**Simple allowlist approach.** The Claude Code docs describe PreToolUse as useful for auto-approving safe operations. A community example checks Bash commands against a hardcoded list of safe prefixes such as npm test, git status, and ls, and approves matches. Notably, that example uses the PermissionRequest hook rather than PreToolUse, so the two hook types are worth comparing for your use case.

**Denylist with daily limits.** yes-claudio installs a PreToolUse hook that returns allow for every permission prompt, unless the command matches the denylist, in which case it returns ask. It is MIT-licensed, but it adds a paid tier and a daily approval cap, so it is not a fully free option. Its design is fail-safe: any internal error returns ask, so Claude Code never auto-approves silently on a crash.

**Agent-callable.** This tool gained a --claude flag that outputs the exact JSON Claude Code expects, and it parses the full shell AST so that chained pipes and conditionals are evaluated as a whole.

**Caveat on auto-approval.** A community write-up notes that WebFetch can send data in query parameters, so a hook that approves everything can miss exfiltration. Its workaround auto-allows clean URLs and prompts when query parameters are present.

None of the results describe a tool that observes your approvals and automatically adds them to a trusted list. If that is what you need, chook's rule-building workflow is the nearest starting point, or you could write a small hook that logs approved commands and proposes allow rules from that log.

Entire is Thomas Dohmke's startup, and its first product is an open-source CLI called Checkpoints that records AI agent sessions alongside Git commits.

**Background and funding**
- Dohmke, who ran GitHub from 2021 until his 2025 departure, leads a team of roughly 15 people drawn from GitHub and Atlassian. The team plans to grow past 30 engineers.
- Per one profile, the company was announced on February 10, 2026, with a $60M seed round at a $300M valuation, led by Felicis. The first product is Checkpoints, an open-source (MIT) CLI.

**What the CLI does**
- It runs inside a Git repository and installs hooks for Git and supported agents. It records the context behind agent-assisted code changes. That context includes prompts, inspected files, tool calls, and intermediate attempts.
- Captured sessions are stored as Checkpoints and linked to commits. Checkpoints are linked to commits without adding noise to your normal Git history.
- Checkpoint metadata lives on a separate branch. Permanent session metadata is kept on a dedicated, hidden branch named entire/checkpoints/v1. By default that branch pushes to your code remote, though a separate Checkpoint Remote can hold it in another repository (per the docs).
- During active sessions, the tool uses temporary shadow branches for code snapshots, which lets you rewind to an earlier state if an agent makes a mistake (per one write-up).
- Documented CLI features include rewinding to earlier Checkpoints during a session and resuming prior agent sessions instead of starting over. The CLI also searches past checkpoints, sessions, and commits, and it provides JSON output for automation and agent workflows.
- Supported agents include Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot CLI, according to one profile.

**Bigger picture**
- Entire describes itself as a developer platform for recording and managing AI coding sessions. It serves as an observability and audit layer for code generated by AI agents.
- The CLI is the first piece. One profile says the full platform, including a git-compatible database and a semantic reasoning layer, was promised for later in 2026. Another report notes that the user interface is still under development, though some functions for visualizing checkpoints exist. The team mainly focuses on the command-line experience for now.

The sources are mostly secondary write-ups plus Entire's own docs, so the product details may change as the project evolves. The official docs at docs.entire.io are the best place to check current commands.

content.content:
**What Jev is:** Jev is the first System One model from TypeSafe AI, released September 15, 2026. It doesn't generate text. It reads your application state and returns decisions: a choice, a score, or a probability, each with a confidence value. The page describes these as "type-safe answers."

**Request format:** You send a `POST` to `https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with a bearer token. The body includes:
- `model`: `jev-latest` (currently resolves to jev-1.13.0)
- `state`: plain text or structured JSON
- `questions`: a map of named questions, each using one of three types:
  - **`noul`**: a yes/no probability from 0 to 1
  - **`choice`**: picks one option from a `criteria` map and returns a probability distribution plus confidence
  - **`score`**: grades the state on an ordered scale you define, returning per-level probabilities, confidence, and a legend

Answers come back keyed by question name, and all questions on one state are evaluated in parallel.

**Pricing:** $0.042 per million input tokens. Output tokens are free.

**Latency:** 70–500 ms typical according to the official figures. Community measurements are reported at 70–300 ms. Adding questions adds almost no latency.

**Limits:**
- Context of about 64k tokens for state plus all questions (about 32k for state plus the longest question)
- Roughly 250k tokens/s and 1,200 requests/min, subject to change during early access
- Error codes: 401 (auth), 422 (validation), 429 (rate limit), 529 (overloaded)

**Free tier:** The page doesn't mention one. Access is by early-access waitlist at typesafe.ai, followed by an API key from the console.

**SDKs:**
- Official: `typesafe-sdk` for Python 3.10+, and `@typesafe-ai/sdk` for Node 20+
- Community clients exist for Rust, Ruby, Go, and Elixir
- An agent skill lets coding assistants call the API directly

**Example code (illustrative sketch, not the page's sample):**

```json
{
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "state": "Customer reports payouts failing for 3 days.",
  "questions": {
    "is_urgent": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Does this convey urgency?" },
    "department": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
      "criteria": {
        "billing": "Payments, invoicing, refunds",
        "technical": "Bugs, outages, integrations"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Use cases listed:**
- **Routing and triage:** sending tickets, prompts, or jobs to the right team, model, or agent
- **Guardrails and safety:** screening prompts and outputs for injection and policy violations, and escalating when confidence falls below a threshold. This is the closest match to your agent permission-gating interest. The page doesn't use the term "permission gating."
- **Agent supervision:** choosing tools, compacting context, or detecting a stuck agent, while an LLM handles generation
- **Real-time decisions:** control loops for games, browser automation, voice, and robotics
- **Search and reranking:** scoring candidates before they reach a downstream LLM
- **Batch classification:** tagging and filtering large volumes in parallel

**Caveat:** The page says a model can still give high confidence to a wrong but valid option, so it recommends confidence thresholds and a fallback path for low-confidence results. Figures are early-access values and may change. Check the official models page before relying on them.

Here's what the search turned up. Coverage of Invariant is thin, and most of the 2026 commentary comes from vendors who sell competing gateways, so treat their comparisons with caution.

**The general pattern: a policy layer between agents and tools**
- Permit.io describes its MCP gateway as a trust and enforcement layer that handles identity, delegated trust, fine-grained authorization, and consent. It frames the core question as which agent may act, for whom, under what policy, and with what oversight. (Vendor blog.)
- Permit also argues for tiered trust: low-risk reads could be automatic, writes need stronger policy, and destructive actions go to an approval gate. (Vendor blog.)
- A PolicyLayer glossary describes the gateway as a point where each tool call is checked against policy before it runs. It also lists per-person tokens and tool filtering as features. (Vendor page.)
- Docker's own docs say the MCP gateway is governed through Cedar policies and default-denies governed activity. Admins can approve servers, require approval for tool calls, and restrict host-run servers. (Official docs.)

**Runlayer**
- TechCrunch's launch coverage (November 2025) describes Runlayer as a gateway bundled with threat detection, observability, and permissions tied to Okta and Entra. It maps agent permissions onto each human user's permissions. (Press coverage.)
- A Speakeasy comparison describes Runlayer as an MCP gateway paired with an endpoint agent. Every request goes through a single-tenant AWS gateway that authenticates, authorizes, scans, and logs it. (Competitor blog, so it has an interest.)
- Runlayer is now in a legal dispute. It sued Rippling, alleging that Rippling copied its MCP gateway, and Rippling denies this and says it is launching its own gateway. (Mezha, citing TechCrunch.)
- A MintMCP comparison claims Runlayer's ML threat-detection accuracy figures come from its own documentation. Treat those numbers as unverified.

**Docker MCP Gateway**
- Docker's open-source gateway runs each MCP server in an isolated container, injects credentials at call time, and logs calls. (Official docs and secondary summaries.)
- Its richer governance layer, MCP Gateway as part of Docker AI Governance, is invite-only and requires contacting sales. (Official docs.)
- One independent review notes that container isolation doesn't make third-party servers or granted permissions trustworthy. It also warns that a descriptive tool name isn't an authorization control. (anavem.com.)

**Lasso**
- Lasso launched its open-source MCP Gateway in April 2025. It acts as a proxy that applies configurable security filters to requests and responses, including PII masking through Presidio. (Press release and secondary coverage.)
- A 2026 MintMCP comparison describes Lasso as security-first, with threat detection for prompt injection and data exfiltration and a plugin architecture. Its emphasis is detection and guardrails more than fine-grained policy, though that's the vendor's framing.

**Invariant**
- The only material I found was Invariant's mcp-scan project. Its gateway wraps MCP server commands in your config files and logs and analyzes traffic, with guardrail enforcement. (DeepWiki summary of the repo.)
- I found no 2026 coverage of Invariant's gateway as a commercial permissions product, so I can't confirm its current status.

**Where this leaves the category**
- The main line of differentiation is: Docker is policy-as-code and container isolation; Runlayer is identity-mapped permissions plus threat scanning; Lasso is open-source guardrails; Invariant is runtime inspection tooling.
- Several sources note that the MCP specification treats authorization as optional, so something has to enforce it around the server. (NeuralTrust, a vendor blog.)

I did not verify funding, pricing, or current product status for any of these companies beyond what's cited above.

**neatHack: AI Agent Hackathon (by neatlogs)**

**Dates & format**
- October 10–12, 2026, online
- Kickoff call: Oct 10, 9:00 AM IST. Hackathon begins: Oct 10, 12:30 PM IST
- Submissions: Oct 12, 7:00–11:55 PM IST (planned close; final cutoff announced on Discord)
- Winners announced: Oct 16

**Track**
- One track: build an AI agent, or a team of agents, that completes a substantial task from start to finish.
- Focus areas: planning, tool use, state, context, execution, recovery, verification, and iteration.
- Example tasks (not separate tracks, and not required): fixing a GitHub issue, researching a question with cited sources, monitoring a running system, multi-agent coordination, and working while the environment changes.

**Required tools**
Your project must use all three:
- **neatlogs:** trace agent runs and use them to improve the agent.
- **Entire:** give your coding agent repository context (checkpoints, entire-graph).
- **cfo.ai:** plan the agent's business (pricing, costs, revenue, runway) and include the plan in your submission. Signup requires a card, which you should cancel right away in Settings → Billing.

**Sponsors & partners**
- Sponsors: cfo.ai, Entire, Dodo Payments, AWS, TheVibeFounder, Crustdata, Orchestrator.inc
- The page doesn't mention TypeSafe or Jev, so I can't confirm either as a sponsor.

**Prizes ($19,000 total including credits)**
- 1st: $2,000 cash + $5,000 Dodo Payments credits
- 2nd: $1,000 cash + $3,000 Dodo Payments credits
- 3rd: $500 cash + $1,000 Dodo Payments credits
- Community winner: $500 cash (can be won alongside a top-three placement)
- Each winner: 3 months of neatlogs Pro (worth $1,500)
- Credits: AWS allowance ($25 per team, first 350 teams to complete web check-in); Crustdata 5,000 credits for all participants; LiteLLM model budget ($20 per team)

**Submission requirements**
- Submit by quoting the official neatlogs post on X with your team name, project name, public repo, and demo.
- Public repository with commits dated during the hackathon.
- Evidence the judges can check: a before/after run comparison (neatlogs traces), links or screenshots of neatlogs traces, Entire checkpoints or entire-graph output, a cfo.ai business plan, a run showing recovery from a failed action, and links tagged #neatHack showing you built in public.
- The page doesn't explicitly say the demo video must be posted on X, only that the submission post includes the demo.

**Judging criteria (weighted, out of 100)**
- The agent: 30%
- Use of neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai: 25%
- Demo video (clarity in explaining the agent and tool use): 20%
- Building in public: 15%
- Usefulness and originality: 10%

**Judges:** Haimantika Mitra, Abhi Singh, Prateek Karnal, Ajay Yadav, Akshay Hangloo

**Mentors:** Karan Pargal, Rohan Mukherjee, Chetan Raj, Ankush Dharkar, Rithvik K

**Not covered:** The FAQ lists questions on team rules, conduct rules, and pre-event building, but the answers aren't included in the page text.

I didn't find a coding agent that ships a per-agent "trust score" with automatic permission revocation on failure. The results describe the pattern in general terms, mostly from enterprise and research sources.

**Closest match: graduated autonomy.** An AWS Architecture blog post describes a pattern where agents gain broader permissions through sustained reliability and lose them when performance drops. It is built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, DynamoDB, and CodePipeline. This post describes graduated autonomy, an architectural pattern in which agents earn expanded permissions through sustained reliability and lose them when performance degrades. It is a reference architecture, not a shipped coding-agent feature.

**Research on earned trust in Claude Code.** Secondhand summaries of Anthropic's February 2026 study, "Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice," report that newer Claude Code users, under 50 sessions, reach for full auto-approve roughly 20% of the time. By 750 sessions, that climbs past 40%. The same summary reports that from August to December, Claude Code's success rate on the hardest internal tasks doubled while average human interventions per session fell from 5.4 to 3.3. I could not check these numbers against Anthropic's original paper, so verify them there before relying on them.

**Ladder-of-trust proposals.** NeuBird's August 2026 framing treats privileges as incremental, with reversible actions first. NeuBird names autonomous rollback as the first rung, because undoing a change proven to have caused an incident is a well-scoped, reversible action. This is aimed at production operations rather than coding agents specifically.

**What coding tools actually ship.** Claude Code has a multi-mode permission system: standard, plan, an auto or classifier-based mode, and bypass, according to one review. That is a user-selected mode, not a trust score that adjusts over time. Security write-ups from 2026 recommend that you locate the setting that controls autonomous action, set it to the most restrictive option you can tolerate, and re-check it after every major tool update. The page excerpt I have cuts off before the detailed per-event sections for PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest, and Stop, so I can't give their full input schemas. Below is what the visible text supports, with gaps marked.

## When each event fires

| Event | When it fires | Can block? |
| :- | :- | :- |
| `PreToolUse` | Before a tool call executes | Yes |
| `PermissionRequest` | When a tool call needs a permission decision | Exit 2 isn't honored. Deny via the `decision` object |
| `PostToolUse` | After a tool call succeeds | No. The tool already ran |
| `PostToolUseFailure` | After a tool call fails | No |
| `PostToolBatch` | After a full batch of parallel tool calls resolves, before the next model call | Yes. Stops the loop |
| `Stop` | When Claude finishes responding | Yes. Prevents stopping and continues the conversation |
| `StopFailure` | When the turn ends due to an API error | No |
| `PermissionDenied` | When auto mode denies a tool call | No |

## Input fields

Every event receives these common fields (command hooks read them from stdin; HTTP hooks get them as the POST body):

`session_id`, `prompt_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `scratchpad_dir`, `permission_mode`, `hook_event_name`

Tool events add `tool_name`, `tool_input`, and `tool_use_id`. For example, a PreToolUse Bash call:

```json
{
  "hook_event_name": "PreToolUse",
  "tool_name": "Bash",
  "tool_input": { "command": "npm test", "timeout": 120000 },
  "tool_use_id": "toolu_01ABC123..."
}
```

`Stop` and `SubagentStop` provide `last_assistant_message`, which is more reliable than reading `transcript_path`, since the transcript may lag the current turn.

*The full input schemas for PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, and Stop aren't in the excerpt.*

## Decision output

**PreToolUse** uses `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision` with `allow`, `deny`, `ask`, or `defer`, plus `permissionDecisionReason`. It can also set `updatedInput` to rewrite tool arguments.

```json
{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
    "permissionDecision": "deny",
    "permissionDecisionReason": "Database writes are not allowed"
  }
}
```

**PermissionRequest** uses `hookSpecificOutput.decision.behavior` (`allow` or `deny`). When allowing, it can include `updatedInput`.

```json
{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "PermissionRequest",
    "decision": {
      "behavior": "allow",
      "updatedInput": { "command": "npm run lint" }
    }
  }
}
```

The excerpt doesn't mention `updatedPermissions`, so I can't confirm its shape.

**PostToolUse** uses a top-level `decision: "block"` with `reason`. It can also use `updatedToolOutput` to replace the tool's result.

**Stop** uses a top-level `decision: "block"` with `reason` to keep Claude working. `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` gives feedback that continues the conversation. Exit code 2 also prevents stopping.

```json
{
  "decision": "block",
  "reason": "Test suite must pass before proceeding"
}
```

**Universal fields** work on any event: `continue: false` with `stopReason` halts Claude entirely, and `systemMessage` shows a warning to the user.

## HTTP hook type

Yes, `type: "http"` exists. Its fields are:

- `url` (required): where to POST the event JSON
- `headers`: values can interpolate env vars listed in `allowedEnvVars`
- `allowedEnvVars`: required for any env var interpolation
- `onFailure`: `"continue"` (default) or `"block"`

```json
{
  "type": "http",
  "url": "http://localhost:8080/hooks/pre-tool-use",
  "timeout": 30,
  "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer $MY_TOKEN" },
  "allowedEnvVars": ["MY_TOKEN"]
}
```

A 2xx response with a JSON body uses the same output schema as command hooks. HTTP hooks can't block through status codes alone. A non-2xx status or connection failure is a non-blocking error unless `onFailure` is `"block"`.

content.text:
# Solo License: plan for the hackathon

**Short answer:** don't keep the refund demo, and don't start a brand-new idea. Keep the engine you already built (earned, revocable, priced trust) and put a new face on it: **a coding agent whose autonomy is earned**. Three findings point to this. The rest is the plan.

---

## 1. Three findings that change the plan

**A. The judging rubric (from [neatlogs.com/hackathon](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon))**

| Criterion | Weight | What it means for us |
|---|---|---|
| The agent | **30%** | They want "an agent that completes a substantial task end to end". A permission gate on its own is not an agent. |
| neatlogs + Entire + cfo.ai | 25% | Entire is built for coding-agent sessions (checkpoints, rewind). With the refund idea it was forced in. With coding it fits naturally. |
| Demo video | 20% | It has to be clear and live. Swyam said it himself: the current demo looks "hard coded / mock". |
| Building in public | 15% | Post on X with #neatHack today. |
| Usefulness/originality | 10% | |

The rubric also lists evidence the judges will check: a **before/after run comparison**, neatlogs traces, Entire checkpoints, a cfo.ai plan, and **a run that recovers from a failed action**. The example tasks include "fixing a GitHub issue".

**B. Your biggest competitor is Claude Code itself.** Anthropic launched **auto mode** in March 2026. A classifier checks each action before it runs and blocks risky ones. According to The Register, it became the default for Pro/Max/Team in August ([claude.com blog](https://claude.com/fr/blog/auto-mode), [TechRadar](https://techradar.com/pro/anthropic-gives-claude-code-new-auto-mode-which-lets-it-choose-its-own-permissions), [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/a/5285326)). If your pitch is "auto-allow trusted commands", a judge will immediately say "Claude already does that". **Prepare your answer to this before anything else** (section 3).

**C. "Jeff" is Jev.** It is the System One model from **TypeSafe AI**, released September 15, 2026 ([jevapi.dev](https://jevapi.dev/)):
- It doesn't generate text. It returns typed outputs: `noul` (probability 0–1), `choice` (a probability distribution over the options), and `score` (a rubric level).
- Vendor figures: 70–500 ms latency, $0.042 per million input tokens, output free. Early access through a waitlist.
- Caveat: a paper titled ["Type-Safe Is Not Error-Free"](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.26758) shows that a valid option can still be the wrong one. The mentor's grey-area → human-in-the-loop idea is the right mitigation.

---

## 2. Decision: what to build and what not to

| Option | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Refund / support agent (current) | ❌ Don't demo it | Mentor said avoid it, judges won't relate, it looks like a mock |
| PR review / merge bot | ❌ | Very crowded: CodeRabbit, Copilot review. "Just another review bot" will be the instant reaction |
| MCP gateway | ❌ | Mentor said it isn't needed: hooks can call your API directly (Claude Code has an `http` hook type). The space is enterprise-crowded too: [Runlayer](https://techcrunch.com/2025/11/17/mcp-ai-agent-security-startup-runlayer-launches-with-8-unicorns-11m-from-khoslas-keith-rabois-and-felicis), [Docker MCP Gateway](https://docs.docker.com/ai/mcp-gateway/), [Lasso](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250417840621/en), [Permit.io](https://www.permit.io/blog/announcing-permit-mcp-gateway) |
| **Coding agent with earned trust + an over-edit guard** | ✅ **Build this** | Mentor's suggestion, a rubric example task, a natural fit for Entire, and it reuses about 60% of the engine |

**New one-liner:** *"Your coding agent earns autonomy per action type from verified results in your repo, loses it the moment something breaks, and gets stopped when it over-edits."*

---

## 3. Competition, and how you are different

| Competitor | What it does | Where it falls short |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code auto mode | Stateless risk classifier per action | It doesn't remember whether similar actions worked before. It doesn't verify outcomes, doesn't revoke, and has no audit trail or economics |
| [chook](https://tangled.org/burrito.space/chook), [yes-claudio](https://pypi.org/project/yes-claudio/0.1.5/), [agent-callable](https://tech.evaneos.com/agent-callable-skip-the-boring-approvals-in-claude-code-2ddb21dc2afb) | Static allow/deny lists | No learning from outcomes, no demotion |
| [unasked](https://pypi.org/project/unasked/), over-reach-detector, moyu skills | Scope-drift / over-edit detection | Detect only. Repeat offending doesn't reduce the agent's autonomy |
| [AWS "graduated autonomy"](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/closing-the-ai-agent-trust-gap-with-graduated-autonomy/) | The same idea, as a reference architecture | Not a shipped tool, and not for coding agents |

I found no shipped coding tool that does **outcome-based** trust with automatic revocation. That gap is your originality.

**Line to say to the judges:**
> "Auto mode asks: *is this action dangerous?* Solo License asks: *has this agent **earned** this kind of action **in this repo**, and did it actually work?*"

Position it as complementary to auto mode, not as a replacement.

---

## 4. Answer to the mentor's main question: "how many calls?"

Don't call on every edit. There are three trigger points, and most decisions never touch an LLM:

1. **`PermissionRequest` hook.** It fires only when Claude would have shown a prompt anyway, so edits that are already allowed never call you.
   - Fast path: look up `(repo, action class)` in the trust table. Deterministic, a few ms.
   - Jev is called only for an unknown command, using `choice` (which action class) and `noul` (destructive/irreversible?).
   - If the probability lands in the grey zone (say 0.35–0.65), ask the human.
2. **`Stop` hook, once per turn.** Send `git diff` plus the original request to Jev with `score` ("is the diff proportionate to the request, 1–5?").
   - On a low score, return `decision: block` with a reason ("revert the unrelated changes in X and Y"). The agent then trims the diff itself.
   - This is the mentor's over-editing idea, at turn granularity rather than per edit.
3. **Outcome signals: tests fail, `PostToolUseFailure`, or a revert happens.** That action class is demoted to L0, a commit goes into the ledger, and Entire rewinds to the checkpoint.

The **action class** (for example `test-run`, `install-dep`, `git-write`, `delete`, `deploy`) is your existing task class. Trust is earned per class, which is the same architecture you have today.

---

## 5. What stays, what changes (no code changes in this step, mapping only)

- **Reuse as-is:** `domain/trust.py` (Beta posterior, break-even, runs needed), `domain/license.py` (levels), `services/git_ledger.py`, policy versions, `services/economics.py`, the neatlogs client/tracer, `detections.py`, the evidence page, `faults/injector.py` (for demo fault injection), and the FastAPI and React shell.
- **New:**
  - three hook endpoints (permission, stop, outcome)
  - an action classifier (rules first, Jev as fallback)
  - a diff-scope checker
  - one `solo-license init` command that writes `.claude/settings.json` hooks
- **Hide from the demo** (no need to delete): intake, Stripe, orders, CSV onboarding.

**For the 30% "agent" criterion:** frame it as two agents. A worker (Claude Code in headless mode) takes a GitHub issue through to a fix and an opened PR. The Solo License supervisor handles plan, gate, verify (tests + scope), recover (rewind + retry with feedback), and trust update. That covers planning, verification, recovery and iteration, which are exactly the rubric's focus areas.

---

## 6. Demo story (2–3 min, live terminal)

1. **The problem (15s):** "Ask before changes" means 40 approvals. "Full access" means fear. Show the approval counter.
2. **Earning trust:** a fresh repo starts at zero trust. Approve `npm test` 2–3 times. The ledger commit `license(test-run): L0→L1` appears, and from then on it is auto-allowed.
3. **Over-edit caught:** for a one-line bug, the agent changes 50 lines. The Stop hook blocks it ("scope 1/5, 3 unrelated files"), and the agent trims it to a 4-line diff. Show the neatlogs trace.
4. **Failure → demotion → recovery:** an auto-allowed action breaks the tests (use the fault injector). That class instantly drops to L0, Entire rewinds to the checkpoint, and the evidence page shows what happened.
5. **Before/after:** the same 5 issues, with and without Solo License. Show approvals asked, over-edited lines, and incidents. This one table is the "before/after run comparison" from the required evidence.
6. **Economics:** cfo.ai covers per-dev pricing, approval minutes saved, and incident cost. The break-even formula stays the same.

---

## 7. Timeline (submission Mon 12 Oct, 7:00–11:55 PM IST)

No install.Get it →","url":"https://skillselion.com/guides/claude-code-plugins-guide"}]

Claude Code plugins are packages that bundle several extension types, and you install them through a marketplace with the `/plugin` command.

**What a plugin contains.** The official docs describe plugins as extensions that extend Claude Code with skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers. One guide adds that plugins can include skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, LSP servers, background monitors, themes, and default settings. In the file layout, skills sit in `skills/` directories, each containing a `SKILL.md` file with YAML frontmatter and instructions, hooks live in `hooks/hooks.json`, and MCP servers are declared in `.mcp.json`.

**Marketplaces.** A marketplace is a catalog of plugins that someone else has created and shared. Adding one is separate from installing: adding the marketplace registers the catalog so you can browse what's available. No plugins are installed yet. The official catalog, claude-plugins-official, is automatically available when you start Claude Code.

**Install commands.** Typical usage looks like this:
- Install from the official marketplace: `/plugin install context7@claude-plugins-official`
- Add a community marketplace: `/plugin marketplace add <owner>/<repo>`
- Test a local plugin without installing it: `claude --plugin-dir ./my-plugin`

Running `/plugin` with no arguments opens an interactive menu where you can browse marketplaces, install, disable, or uninstall without memorizing names. Install scope is configurable: one source describes user scope, project scope (which adds to `.claude/settings.json` and is shared with everyone who clones the repo), and local scope.

**Plugins versus standalone skills and MCP.** Standalone configuration lives in `.claude/`, while plugins are distributed. One source puts it this way: plugins are namespaced, versioned, and shareable through marketplaces. Namespacing matters because plugin skills are invoked as `/plugin-name:command`, which avoids conflicts. Another guide suggests that skills win on simplicity: one folder, no marketplace, works across Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and the Agent SDK. Default to a skill when the job is knowledge, conventions, or a repeatable procedure.

**Usage notes.** After installing, one guide says you can run `/reload-plugins`. Skills appear under their namespace. Agents show in `/agents`. Hooks start firing. MCP servers start in the background. For development, after every edit, run `/reload-plugins` to pick up changes. One guide also notes that if the `/plugin` command is not available, update Claude Code to the latest version.

**Caveat:** Most of these sources are third-party guides rather than official documentation. The one official page I found covers only the marketplace basics. Plugin counts and version requirements vary between sources, so check the official plugins reference at code.claude.com for current details.

# Option 1 (refund) vs Option 2 (coding agent), plus hooks vs MCP vs plugin

**On your new message: yes, keep hooks. Hooks should do the enforcement, and a plugin is how you ship them.** The reasons are in section 4.

## 1. If you keep the existing refund product: how to position it

The space is crowded. Intercom Fin, Decagon, Sierra, Netomi, Lorikeet and Fini all handle refunds already. What they all share is a **static rule**, for example "auto-approve refunds up to $50, a human reviews anything above" ([Fin guide](https://fin.ai/learn/ai-guardrails-customer-service), [eesel](https://www.eesel.ai/blog/ai-for-refund-requests)). Netomi has per-intent autonomy levels, but someone sets those by hand ([Fini comparison](https://www.usefini.com/blog/top-10-ai-agents-for-handling-refunds-returns-cancellations-automatically)).

**Don't compete as a support agent. Position as the layer underneath it:**

> **"A credit limit for AI agents."** A new agent starts with a low limit. Verified results raise the limit, and a single failure cuts it.

It is not another support bot. It is an autonomy controller that sits under any agent (Fin, Decagon, or your own). Everyone else's $50 threshold is something a person types in. Yours moves on its own, based on evidence and your break-even economics.

**How to make the existing product better:**
- **Put a static $50 rule next to Solo License on the same 500 tickets.** Show the outcome as a cost graph: manual reviews, mistakes, money lost. This is your strongest proof point.
- **Show the read-back moment live.** The tool says "success", the database disagrees, the agent recovers. Nobody else verifies like this.
- **Add a Zendesk/Intercom webhook.** You already have `POST /api/inbox`. It changes the story from "replace their bot" to "plug in behind their bot".

**Honest risk:** the mentor advised against it, judges find it harder to relate to, and this hackathon asks for an agent that completes a task, not a CFO-style workflow. **My call: show refunds as one slide ("the same engine works for payments too") and don't make it the demo.**

## 2. If you go with the coding agent: the full competition

| Category | Players | What they lack that you have |
|---|---|---|
| Built-in permission modes | Claude Code auto mode (risk classifier), Codex approval modes, Cursor allowlist | Stateless. They don't learn from outcomes or revoke on failure |
| Hook allowlists | [chook](https://tangled.org/burrito.space/chook), [yes-claudio](https://pypi.org/project/yes-claudio/0.1.5/), [agent-callable](https://tech.evaneos.com/agent-callable-skip-the-boring-approvals-in-claude-code-2ddb21dc2afb) | Static rules, no trust ladder |
| Over-edit detectors | [unasked](https://pypi.org/project/unasked/), over-reach-detector, moyu skills | They detect over-edits, but the agent's autonomy never changes |
| MCP gateways | [Runlayer](https://techcrunch.com/2025/11/17/mcp-ai-agent-security-startup-runlayer-launches-with-8-unicorns-11m-from-khoslas-keith-rabois-and-felicis), [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/ai/mcp-gateway/), [Lasso](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250417840621/en), [Permit.io](https://www.permit.io/blog/announcing-permit-mcp-gateway) | Enterprise and identity-focused. They only see MCP calls, not Bash or file edits |
| PR bots | CodeRabbit, Copilot review | They act after the code is written. You act while it's being written |
| Pattern only | [AWS graduated autonomy](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/closing-the-ai-agent-trust-gap-with-graduated-autonomy/) | A reference architecture, not a product |

**Your gap: nobody combines all three of these:**
1. Trust earned per action class, per repo
2. Automatic demotion on failure
3. Over-editing that reduces autonomy

## 3. Hooks vs MCP vs plugin: how each would work

| | What it is | Can it enforce? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MCP server** | Tools the model can choose to call | ❌ No. The model decides whether to call an MCP tool, so a gate built on it is optional, and the agent can skip it | Read-only extras only |
| **MCP gateway** | A proxy in front of MCP servers | Only for MCP traffic. `rm -rf`, `git push` and file edits never pass through it | ❌ Wrong layer |
| **Hooks** | Claude Code itself runs them on every event (an `http` hook can call your API directly) | ✅ The agent can't bypass them | **The core** |
| **Plugin** | A package of hooks + skills + slash commands + an optional MCP server, installed with `/plugin install` ([docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/discover-plugins?m=1)) | Hooks inside it enforce | **How you distribute** |

**Final shape:**
- **Enforcement = hooks.** `PermissionRequest` gates actions, `Stop` checks over-edits once per turn, and outcome signals (tests failing, `PostToolUseFailure`, reverts) demote the action class.
- **Distribution = a Claude Code plugin.** One command, `/plugin install solo-license`, sets up all the hooks. This is your "one command setup" demo line.
- **Optional MCP = read-only.** For example, `trust_status()` lets the agent ask "what can I do here without approval?" so it plans around its limits. That's a nice extra, not a requirement.
- **Later:** Codex has a Claude-compatible `PreToolUse` hooks format, and Cursor has `beforeShellExecution`. So the claim "same trust API, many agents" is realistic. Cursor's hooks are reported to be flaky in its own forum, so for the demo, **Claude Code only**.

## 4. What to do so it works best

1. **One surface, one agent:** Claude Code + hooks, packaged as a plugin. No MCP gateway, no merge bot.
2. **Keep the fast path deterministic.** Look up the trust table and answer in milliseconds. Call Jev only for unknown commands and for the once-per-turn diff check. This directly answers the mentor's "how many calls?" question.
3. **Fail-safe defaults.** If your API is down or Jev times out, the hook returns `ask`, never `allow`. Say this explicitly in the video. It's a strong trust point.
4. **Trust key = (repo, action class)**, not individual commands. `npm test`, `pytest` and `cargo test` all count as `test-run`. Without this, trust takes forever to build up.
5. **A demotion must be visible:** a ledger commit, an Entire rewind, and a neatlogs trace, all three in the same frame.
6. **Before/after with numbers.** Run 5 issues with and without the plugin: approvals asked, diff lines, incidents. This is the required evidence and the strongest slide.
7. **Refunds become one slide:** "the same engine already runs payments", with a screenshot of the existing app. Your past work becomes proof of the platform claim and isn't wasted.

**Bottom line:** hooks are the engine, the plugin is how it's packaged, and MCP is at most a read-only extra. The refund product becomes evidence of the platform, not the demo.

**Sources:** [Fin guardrails](https://fin.ai/learn/ai-guardrails-customer-service) · [eesel refunds](https://www.eesel.ai/blog/ai-for-refund-requests) · [Fini refund tools comparison](https://www.usefini.com/blog/top-10-ai-agents-for-handling-refunds-returns-cancellations-automatically) · [Lorikeet guardrails](https://www.lorikeetcx.ai/articles/what-are-ai-guardrails-for-customer-service) · [Stripe agent toolkit](https://www.deeplearning.ai/the-batch/stripe-builds-ecommerce-agent-toolkit-for-ai-to-securely-spend-money) · [Fystack spend guardrails](https://fystack.io/blog/6-guardrails-to-limit-ai-agent-spending-on-payment-rails) · [Claude Code plugins](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/discover-plugins?m=1) · [plugin guide](https://fast.io/resources/claude-code-plugins-development-guide/) · [Cursor CLI hooks thread](https://forum.cursor.com/t/cursor-cli-hooks/148511) · [Cursor hooks not firing](https://forum.cursor.com/t/hooks-not-firing-cannot-have-guardrails/168407) · [Codex hooks (developertoolkit)](https://developertoolkit.ai/pl/developer-scorecard-guide/agent-hooks/) · [Runlayer](https://techcrunch.com/2025/11/17/mcp-ai-agent-security-startup-runlayer-launches-with-8-unicorns-11m-from-khoslas-keith-rabois-and-felicis) · [Docker MCP Gateway](https://docs.docker.com/ai/mcp-gateway/) · [Lasso](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250417840621/en) · [Permit.io](https://www.permit.io/blog/announcing-permit-mcp-gateway) · [AWS graduated autonomy](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/closing-the-ai-agent-trust-gap-with-graduated-autonomy/) · [unasked](https://pypi.org/project/unasked/) · [chook](https://tangled.org/burrito.space/chook) · [yes-claudio](https://pypi.org/project/yes-claudio/0.1.5/) · [agent-callable](https://tech.evaneos.com/agent-callable-skip-the-boring-approvals-in-claude-code-2ddb21dc2afb)
